𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐀𝐜𝐜𝐞𝐥𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐢𝐬 𝐚 𝐓𝐫𝐮𝐞 𝐃𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐳𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐦

Everybody knows that decentralization is primarily a software issue. I used to know that too.

However, the deeper we dive into the actual behavior of blockchain networks, the clearer it is that decentralization is actually a matter of data transmission.

An open-source protocol might run on a permissionless basis and use globally distributed validators. Still, as soon as data is transmitted differently depending on its geographical location, decentralization becomes compromised.

And this is exactly what happens in the real world.

𝘈𝘯 𝘪𝘯𝘷𝘪𝘴𝘪𝘣𝘭𝘦 𝘧𝘢𝘤𝘵𝘰𝘳 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘥𝘳𝘪𝘷𝘦𝘴 𝘯𝘦𝘵𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘬𝘴 𝘵𝘰𝘸𝘢𝘳𝘥𝘴 𝘤𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘳𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘻𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯.

Decentralization requires two main criteria to truly persist:

- Firstly, ordinary people must be able to operate validators using regular infrastructure.

- Secondly, those validators have to be globally distributed rather than concentrated in a handful of datacenters located close to key internet exchange points in Europe and North America.

Today, however, the fulfillment of both criteria quietly disappears.

𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘤𝘶𝘭𝘱𝘳𝘪𝘵 𝘣𝘦𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘥 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘱𝘩𝘦𝘯𝘰𝘮𝘦𝘯𝘰𝘯 𝘪𝘴 𝘭𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘯𝘤𝘺.

While latency sounds like a minor issue, once you understand how blockchains function, you see how crucial it is.

Thousands of validators have to stay synced in real-time. Each new block, each attestations, and each piece of information has to cross multiple borders — from continents to cables, from ISPs to relays, — for a consensus to occur.

Now let us imagine two validators.

- One is placed in Frankfurt in a highly-sophisticated datacenter with premium routing and internet exchange peering.

- Another one operates in Nairobi or Manila with a common home or business connection.

The former has the same hardware and software as the latter. Still, the former regularly receives pieces of information faster than the latter — usually by milliseconds, sometimes even seconds.

In a blockchain network, this difference is amplified.

→ The less reliable validator loses connections more frequently.
→ Its responses do not make it to the network in time.
→ Its performance score goes down.
→ Other peers start ignoring connections to this validator.

And this node will eventually become useless for the network merely due to its geographical location.

This is the point that nobody sees.

Geography becomes an invisible burden.

Not because of incompetence of an operator.
Not because the quality of his hardware is inferior.
Just because the network incentivizes the proximity to major internet hubs.

When validators figure out this mechanism, they adapt accordingly.

Node operators in APAC, Africa, and LATAM move infrastructure to the same region — Frankfurt, Virginia, Amsterdam, Singapore.

At first, it looks reasonable.
Then it becomes more natural.

All of a sudden, the idea of decentralization remains, yet operational reality forces the network to focus on a limited number of locations, providers, and routing paths.

This is how centralization happens quietly.
Not by malevolent actions.
By pure incentives.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝘂𝗽𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗱𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗮𝗱𝗱𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺

Usually, people deal with latency issues wrongly.
They try solving the problem by using faster hardware.

- Therefore, operators increase the number of CPUs they use.
- They upgrade memory.
- They acquire higher-end servers.
- They use extra bandwidth.

However, it is crucial to note that when the problem of data transmission through a network exists, faster hardware can help only on the level of network edges.

It is similar to increasing the speed of a car while staying in traffic jams.
Once you cannot overcome your environment anymore, the problem becomes different.

This is where data acceleration comes into play.

𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘪𝘴𝘴𝘶𝘦 𝘪𝘴 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘢𝘣𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘥𝘶𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘰𝘧 𝘧𝘢𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘳 𝘥𝘢𝘵𝘢.

It is about its effective transmission.

𝗢𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗺𝘂𝗺'𝘀 𝘀𝗼𝗹𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺

@get_optimum 's approach lies in addressing decentralization as a propagation problem.

Unlike flooding schemes, which are based on ineffective broadcasting of information between nodes, mump2p makes data transmission more efficient.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗶𝘀 𝗶𝘁 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗻𝘁?

Because when the process of data transmission improves, smaller validators no longer require powerful infrastructure to compete effectively.

As the network becomes friendlier towards geography, the following occurs:

→ A validator placed in São Paulo no longer has to colocate near key internet exchange infrastructure.

→ An operator based in Kenya no longer has to buy a $10,000 server just to be able to establish healthy peer-to-peer connections.

→ An individual staker in Southeast Asia does not have to feel disadvantaged forever.

The outcome, however, is much more profound.

The system starts changing who can participate.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗶𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝘃𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘇𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻?

We tend to speak of decentralization as an ideological goal. Yet, decentralization is merely an engineering prowess.

Once networks reward fast regions and punish slow ones, slow regions disappear.
When smaller operators cannot compete, enterprises come up on top.

When infrastructure focuses on a limited number of locations, a network loses its ability to resist censorship automatically.

This is the way physics and economic incentives work.

The problem of data acceleration is therefore crucial.

Not only because it decreases latency.
Primarily because it helps prevent validator centralization.

Which, ultimately, preserves decentralization.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗱𝘀 𝘁𝗼

I believe that the industry starts realizing something important.

While blockchain infrastructure becomes faster, it is not enough.
The future lies in making distributed systems function fairly around the world.

This implies overcoming geographical barriers, propagation inefficiency, and uneven connections.

Since the participation in a network should depend on living near a major internet hub, the network fails to be decentralized at all.

Optimum solves this problem at the very data transmission stage.
Not by asking operators to invest in more sophisticated hardware.
But by optimizing network's ability to transmit existing data.

And this creates a different dynamic.

✔️ Smaller operators become economically feasible.
✔️ Geographical disadvantages vanish.
✔️ A blockchain network comes closer to true decentralization, not performative.

If you run blockchain infrastructure and tired of the influence of geography on the network performance, check out mump2p at https://t.co/YYRZk7DWPg.

Start building 👉 @get_optimum
